title: Neighbors of Many Faiths
bigQuestion: How can people of many faiths, and people of no faith, live and work together as good neighbors?

story.title: Three Doors, One Food Drive
story.kicker: A church, a mosque and a synagogue on one block fill the same truck with food.
paragraphs: It is a cold Saturday morning in Chicago. On one block stand three buildings. One is a church with a tall steeple. One is a mosque with a green dome. One is a synagogue with a Star of David over the door.
Today the three groups are running a food drive together. Volunteers carry boxes of rice, beans, soup and pasta out to a big white truck. A sign on the truck says: Neighbors Feeding Neighbors.

Amira, age nine, tapes labels on boxes. Her family prays at the mosque. Next to her, Eli stacks cans. He goes to the synagogue. Grace, who goes to the church, counts the boxes and writes the total on a clipboard.

Eli picks up a can of soup and frowns. "Does this one have pork in it?" he asks. "My family keeps kosher, and so does the pantry at our synagogue." Amira nods. "Muslims who eat halal skip pork too." Grace reads the label. "Chicken noodle," she says. "No pork."

By noon the truck is full. The three leaders shake hands. Each group believes different things about God and prayer. Today they found one thing they could do together: make sure their neighbors have enough to eat.
story.think: The children asked each other questions about food. Why do you think asking helped them work together?

lessons.title: Many Buildings, Many Faiths
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago has churches, synagogues, mosques, temples and gurdwaras, where people of many faiths gather.
reading: Take a bus ride across Chicago and look out the window. You will pass churches with steeples and crosses. You may see a synagogue, a mosque with a dome, a Hindu temple, a Buddhist temple and a Sikh gurdwara.

Each building is a *house of worship*. That means a place where people gather to pray, sing, read holy writings and learn. Christians often meet in churches. Jews often meet in synagogues. Muslims often pray in mosques.
Many Hindus and Buddhists visit temples. Sikhs gather in a gurdwara, which means "door of the Guru." Chicago has all of these because people from all over the world have made their homes here.

words.d: a building where people of a faith gather to pray, learn and celebrate
a Sikh house of worship; the name means door of the Guru

look.title: Match the Building
look.text: Picture three buildings. Building 1 has a cross on top. Building 2 has a Star of David by the door. Building 3 has a dome and a tall tower called a minaret.
look.prompt: Which faith group would most likely gather in each building? What clue helped you decide?

check.q: What is a house of worship?
choices: A store that sells holy books
A place where people of a faith gather to pray and learn
check.why: A house of worship is a building where people gather to pray, learn and celebrate their faith.

check.q: Which group gathers in a gurdwara?
check.why: A gurdwara is a Sikh house of worship. Its name means door of the Guru.

check.q: Why does Chicago have houses of worship of so many faiths?
choices: People from all over the world made their homes there
The city built one of each on purpose
Only one faith is allowed in each neighborhood
Every building must change faiths each year
check.why: People came to Chicago from many places and brought their faiths with them.

lessons.title: Inside a Church, Synagogue and Mosque
lessons.mainIdea: Each house of worship has special things inside that show what matters to the people who gather there.
reading: Walk into many churches and you may see a cross, rows of seats called pews, and an altar at the front. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God. The cross reminds them of his death and, they believe, his rising again.

In a synagogue, the most special place is the *ark*, a cabinet on the front wall. Inside are Torah scrolls. The Torah holds the first five books of the Hebrew Bible. Jews read from it aloud in services.

A mosque has an open prayer hall, often with rugs. A small curved space in the wall, the mihrab, shows the direction of Mecca. Muslims face that way when they pray. Many mosques have no chairs, so people can bow and kneel.

words.d: in a synagogue, the cabinet that holds the Torah scrolls
a curved space in a mosque wall that shows which way to face Mecca in prayer

look.title: Three Front Walls
look.text: Wall A has a cabinet with curtains. Behind them are rolled scrolls. Wall B has a curved space shaped like an arch, with rugs on the floor in front. Wall C has a table and a cross above it.
look.prompt: Name the house of worship for each wall. Tell what each special object is used for.

check.q: What is kept inside the ark in a synagogue?
check.why: The ark is the cabinet that holds the Torah scrolls, which are read aloud in services.

check.q: What does the mihrab in a mosque show?
choices: The direction of Mecca for prayer
The time of the next holiday
check.why: The mihrab shows which way to face Mecca, the direction Muslims face when they pray.

check.q: Why do many mosques have open floors with rugs instead of chairs?
choices: Muslims bow and kneel when they pray
check.why: Muslim prayer includes bowing and kneeling, so an open floor with rugs gives room.

lessons.title: A Temple Open to All
lessons.mainIdea: The Bahá'í House of Worship in Wilmette has nine sides and nine doors and welcomes people of every faith.
reading: North of Chicago, in the town of Wilmette, stands a white building covered in lace-like patterns. It is the *Bahá'í House of Worship*. It was finished and opened for worship in 1953, after many years of building.

The building has nine sides and nine doors. Bahá'ís believe that God has sent many teachers, and that people of all religions are one human family. The nine doors are often said to welcome people from every direction.
Inside there are no sermons. People read or sing passages from Bahá'í writings and from the holy books of other faiths. Visitors of any religion, or none, are welcome to sit quietly and listen.

words.d: a nine-sided building in Wilmette, Illinois, open to people of all faiths
a follower of the Bahá'í Faith, which teaches that all people are one family

look.title: The Temple in Numbers
look.cite: Bahá'í House of Worship, Wilmette, Illinois, visitor information
look.prompt: Which number shows up twice? Why might Bahá'ís choose many doors for a building open to all?

check.q: Where is the Bahá'í House of Worship?
check.why: The Bahá'í House of Worship stands in Wilmette, just north of Chicago.

check.q: How many sides and doors does the Bahá'í House of Worship have?
check.why: The building has nine sides and nine doors.

check.q: What do Bahá'ís believe about people of all religions?
choices: Only one group may visit the temple
They must all speak one language
check.why: Bahá'ís believe all people are one human family, so the temple welcomes everyone.

lessons.title: The Parliament of 1893
lessons.mainIdea: In 1893 Chicago hosted the World's Parliament of Religions, where leaders of many faiths spoke to one another.
reading: In 1893 Chicago held a giant world's fair. People came to see new inventions, like the first Ferris wheel. At the same time, the city held a meeting called the *World's Parliament of Religions*.

A parliament is a meeting where people speak and listen. Leaders came from many faiths: Christians, Jews, Hindus, Buddhists, Muslims and others. It was one of the first times so many faiths met in one room.

A Hindu teacher from India named Swami Vivekananda began his talk with the words "Sisters and Brothers of America." The crowd cheered. Many people today remember the Parliament as a first step in faiths learning about one another.

words.d: a meeting of leaders of many faiths held in Chicago in 1893
a meeting where people gather to speak and listen to one another

look.title: Opening Words
look.text: Imagine a huge hall in 1893. Thousands of people wait. A speaker from India walks up. Most listeners have never met a Hindu before. He begins: "Sisters and Brothers of America."
look.prompt: Why do you think the crowd cheered those first words? How might a greeting help strangers listen?

check.q: What happened in Chicago in 1893?
choices: The World's Parliament of Religions met
check.why: The World's Parliament of Religions met in Chicago in 1893, during the world's fair.

check.q: Who began his talk with "Sisters and Brothers of America"?
check.why: Swami Vivekananda, a Hindu teacher from India, opened his talk with those words.

check.q: What is a parliament?
choices: A meeting where people speak and listen
check.why: A parliament is a meeting where people gather to speak and listen.

lessons.title: The Parliament Returns
lessons.mainIdea: Starting in 1993, the Parliament of the World's Religions began meeting again, including more times in Chicago.
reading: One hundred years later, in 1993, people held a new Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago. This time thousands of people came from many more faiths than in 1893.

Since then, the Parliament has met in cities around the world. It came back to Chicago in 2023. People share music, prayers, food and ideas. They talk about problems all faiths care about, like hunger and caring for the earth.

The Parliament does not try to make everyone believe the same thing. Its goal is *interfaith* understanding. That means people of different faiths learning about each other and working together on shared goals.

words.d: between or among people of different religions
knowing what someone else believes and why it matters to them

look.title: Parliaments in Chicago
look.cite: Parliament of the World's Religions, published history
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first and second Parliament? Why might people choose that number?

check.q: What does interfaith mean?
check.why: Interfaith means between or among people of different religions.

check.q: What is the main goal of the Parliament?
choices: To make everyone believe the same thing
To help faiths understand each other and work together
check.why: The Parliament aims for interfaith understanding, not for everyone to believe the same thing.

check.q: In what year did a new Parliament meet in Chicago, 100 years after the first?
check.why: The hundred-year Parliament met in Chicago in 1993.

lessons.title: Faiths Work Together
lessons.mainIdea: Groups of different faiths often join hands on helping projects, like food drives and building homes.
reading: Many faiths teach people to help others. Christians often point to Jesus's teaching to treat others the way you want to be treated. Jews speak of *tzedakah*, which means giving to those in need as a matter of justice.
Muslims give *zakat*, a set share of their wealth for people in need. It is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Sikhs serve free meals to anyone who comes to the gurdwara.
Because helping matters to many faiths, groups often work together. In Chicago, churches, synagogues, mosques and temples have run food pantries, winter coat drives and clean-up days side by side.

words.d: in Judaism, giving to people in need as a matter of justice
in Islam, giving a set share of wealth to people in need; one of the Five Pillars

look.title: A Rule for Treating Others
look.text: Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.
look.prompt: Say this verse in your own words. How could it help a group of neighbors plan a food drive?

check.q: Which word names giving in Judaism?
check.why: Tzedakah is the Jewish word for giving to people in need as a matter of justice.

check.q: Zakat is one of the Five Pillars of which faith?
check.why: Zakat, giving a share of wealth to people in need, is one of the Five Pillars of Islam.

check.q: Why do groups of different faiths often work together to help others?
choices: Their faiths are exactly the same
Helping others matters in many faiths
They want everyone to join one group
check.why: Many faiths teach helping others, so groups can share that goal even when their beliefs differ.

lessons.title: The First Amendment
lessons.mainIdea: The First Amendment says the government may not pick a religion, and people may follow any faith or none.
reading: The United States has a set of rules called the Constitution. In 1791, ten changes were added, called the Bill of Rights. The very first one is the *First Amendment*. It protects freedom of religion.
In plain words, it says two things. First, the government may not set up an official religion or pick one faith over others. Second, the government may not stop people from following their faith.
This means a person may be Christian, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh, Bahá'í, or of any faith. A person may also follow no religion at all. Everyone has the same rights either way.

words.d: the first change to the U.S. Constitution; it protects freedom of religion, speech and more
the right to follow any faith, or none, without the government choosing for you

look.title: The Words About Religion
look.text: Congress, the group that makes national laws, may not set up an official religion. It also may not stop people from freely practicing their religion.
look.cite: First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution (1791), religion clauses, in plain words
look.prompt: What are the two things this part of the First Amendment protects?

check.q: What does the First Amendment say about religion?
choices: The government may not pick a religion, and people may follow any or none
Everyone must follow the same religion
People must tell the government their faith
check.why: The First Amendment keeps the government from picking a religion and protects people's right to follow any faith or none.

check.q: When was the First Amendment added to the Constitution?
check.why: The Bill of Rights, including the First Amendment, was added in 1791.

check.q: Kai does not follow any religion. What does the First Amendment say?
choices: Kai cannot go to public school
Kai has the same rights as everyone
check.why: Freedom of religion includes the right to follow no religion, with the same rights as everyone.

lessons.title: Religion at a Public School
lessons.mainIdea: Public schools teach about religions without telling students what to believe.
reading: A public school is paid for by the government. Because of the First Amendment, a public school may not lead students in prayer or tell them which faith is true.
But public schools may teach *about* religions. That is what this course does. You learn what each faith's followers believe and do, the way you might learn about any big part of history and culture.
Students keep their own freedom too. A student may pray quietly on their own, wear a headscarf or turban, or skip foods their faith does not allow. Teachers try to make room for these needs.

words.d: a school paid for by the government and open to all children
something a person holds to be true

look.title: Teaching or Telling?
look.text: Lesson 1: The teacher says, "Muslims fast during the month of Ramadan. Here is why it matters to them." Lesson 2: The teacher says, "Everyone must fast this month because it is the right thing to do."
look.prompt: Which lesson teaches about religion? Which one tells students what to believe? Explain.

check.q: What may a public school do?
choices: Tell students which faith is true
check.why: Public schools may teach about religions, but may not lead prayer or say which faith is true.

check.q: A student wears a turban to school. What is this?
choices: Part of freely practicing a faith
check.why: Many Sikhs wear a turban as part of their faith, and students keep that freedom at school.

check.q: What is a belief?
choices: Something a person holds to be true
check.why: A belief is something a person holds to be true.

lessons.title: Being a Good Neighbor
lessons.mainIdea: Good neighbors ask kind questions and never tease others about food, clothes or holidays.
reading: Your classmate brings a lunch you have never seen. Another wears a headscarf. A friend misses school for a holiday you do not know. You may feel curious. That is fine! Curious is a great way to learn.

A *respectful* question sounds like this: "What is that holiday? How does your family celebrate it?" It is kind and open. A teasing remark, like "That food looks weird," can hurt and make someone feel left out.

Many faiths teach care for neighbors and strangers. The Hebrew Bible tells people to love the stranger. The Qur'an says people were made into nations and tribes so they could come to know one another.

words.d: showing care for another person's feelings, ideas and ways
a person who lives or learns near you; in many faiths, anyone you meet

look.title: Love the Stranger
look.text: But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
look.prompt: What does this verse ask people to do for a newcomer? What reason does it give?

check.q: Which of these is a respectful question?
choices: Why is your lunch so weird?
Your holiday is not real, right?
How does your family celebrate that holiday?
check.why: Asking how a family celebrates is kind and open. The others tease or put someone down.

check.q: According to Leviticus 19:34, how should people treat the stranger?
check.why: The verse says to love the stranger as yourself, because the people were once strangers in Egypt.

check.q: According to the Qur'an, why were people made into nations and tribes?
choices: So they could come to know one another
So one would rule the rest
check.why: The Qur'an (49:13) says people were made into nations and tribes so they could know one another.

review.q: Which house of worship belongs with Sikhs?
review.why: Sikhs gather in a gurdwara, which means door of the Guru.

review.q: What makes the Bahá'í House of Worship in Wilmette special?
choices: It is open only to Bahá'ís
It has nine doors and welcomes people of all faiths
review.why: The nine-sided Bahá'í House of Worship welcomes visitors of any faith or none.

review.q: Where and when did the first World's Parliament of Religions meet?
review.why: The first World's Parliament of Religions met in Chicago in 1893.

review.q: What is the difference between zakat and tzedakah?
choices: Zakat is a building and tzedakah is a book
Zakat is Muslim giving; tzedakah is Jewish giving
review.why: Both mean giving to people in need. Zakat comes from Islam and tzedakah from Judaism.

review.q: Which rule comes from the First Amendment?
choices: The government must pick one faith
People may follow any religion or none
review.why: The First Amendment protects freedom of religion, including the right to follow no religion.

review.q: What is kept in the ark of a synagogue?
review.why: The ark holds the Torah scrolls, read aloud in Jewish services.

review.q: A classmate skips the pork at lunch. What is a kind thing to do?
choices: Ask kindly if they want to share why
review.why: Some Jews and Muslims do not eat pork. A kind, open question respects them.

review.q: In the story, what did the church, mosque and synagogue do together?
review.why: The three groups kept their own beliefs and worked together on a food drive.
